evidence: The production package is a single flat directory lev/ with exactly 6 files (cli.py, engine.py, loop.py, router.py, types.py, __init__.py) totaling 282 LOC — below the <20-file small-project threshold where flat structure is appropriate, so no flat_dir_issues apply.

File placement matches ownership: types.py holds all frozen dataclasses (8 importers — genuinely core), engine.py holds pure scoring/tokenization primitives, loop.py holds the classification orchestration (5 importers), router.py is a 19-line parsing seam (3 importers), cli.py is the entry point.

Import direction is strictly acyclic and one-way: cli.py -> {loop, router} -> engine -> types; no reciprocal/bidirectional directory edges and no downstream->upstream imports exist in the coupling matrix.
No root-level Python stragglers: all source lives under lev/, and root files (pyproject.toml, README.md, uv.lock) are standard packaging artifacts, not misplaced code.

Directory names are meaningful (engine/loop/router/types/cli) and a developer can predict where to find and put things from the names alone; tests/ mirrors production structure, which is explicitly skipped.

Minor rough edge: loop.py re-exports 10 symbols (91% re-export ratio) and imports math plus Counter it barely uses, blurring its single-responsibility boundary with engine.py — an isolated placement/navigation nit, not a structural mismatch.
package_organization.issues_preventing_higher_score: loop.py accumulates re-exported symbols (Counter, engine helpers, all types) giving it a facade-like profile that slightly obscures whether it is the orchestration module or a second engine; tightening its imports would remove the only placement ambiguity in an otherwise exemplary layout.

package_organization.dimension_character: This is a tiny, single-package project (6 production files, 282 LOC) whose flat lev/ layout is the appropriate structure at this scale, and every file's placement matches its ownership: types are centralized, engine is pure primitives, loop orchestrates, router parses, cli drives. Dependency direction is strictly one-way with no cycles, stragglers, or ambiguous folder names, so a developer can navigate entirely by directory names. The only friction is loop.py's high re-export ratio, which gives it a mild facade profile and slightly blurs the engine/loop boundary.
package_organization.score_rationale: Anchored at 90 = 'mostly coherent with minor placement outliers': the structure is essentially exemplary for a project this size — no thresholded defect (straggler roots, >60% import-affinity mismatch, overloaded >10-file directories, coupling-direction failures) is present. The score sits slightly above the 90 anchor because the single rough edge (loop.py's re-export surface) is cosmetic and navigational rather than a true ownership mismatch, keeping the layout at strong/exemplary rather than merely solid.

evidence: lev/loop.py imports math, collections.Counter, blend/confidence/raw_choice_scores/tokenize from lev.engine, and all four dataclasses from lev.types, then defines only classify() itself — a 91% re-export ratio per structure signals
lev/loop.py:2 imports Counter but never uses it (confirmed unused-import signal), a symptom of the file acting as an accidental re-export hub
issues.suggestion: Staged reorg (single edit, no new folders needed at this size): (1) drop the unused 'from collections import Counter' line; (2) keep only the symbols loop.py actually references in its own code (math, engine helpers, ChoiceQuestion/ScoreQuestion/ChoiceResult/ScoreResult are all genuinely used, so imports stay) — the defect is the unused import and facade-like profile, not the imports themselves; (3) validate with 'uv run ruff check lev/loop.py' and 'uv run pytest tests/'. No directory moves are warranted: with 6 files, introducing subpackages would reduce navigability rather than improve it.
